title: Cohere Fights Daily for AI Computing Power Amid Shortages
summary: Nvidia-backed Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez reveals his startup battles compute shortages daily, contradicting concerns about overbuilt AI infrastructure capacity.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez says his Nvidia-backed startup fights daily to secure AI computing power, contradicting overcapacity fears.
- The Canadian enterprise AI company depends on cloud providers like Azure and CoreWeave for computational resources amid persistent shortages.
- Gomez's comments came during a Japan business expansion trip, following Cohere's recent $5 billion funding round at $20 billion valuation.


Cohere Inc. CEO Aidan Gomez is pushing back hard against industry concerns about overbuilt AI infrastructure, revealing that his Nvidia-backed startup faces a relentless daily struggle to secure the computing power needed to run its enterprise AI operations. Speaking from Tokyo on November 11, 2026, Gomez described a market reality sharply at odds with fears of excess capacity, saying his team must fight continuously for access to computational resources.


## The Reality Behind Compute Scarcity


The Canadian startup, which develops artificial intelligence models for business clients, confronts what the industry calls compute shortages: the computational power required to train and operate large-scale AI models. Without owning its own data centers, Cohere relies entirely on cloud providers including Microsoft Azure and neocloud operators like CoreWeave Inc. to meet its processing demands.


"We really have to fight to get access to compute," Gomez told Bloomberg in an interview during his Japan business expansion trip. "There is a dearth of supply. We need much more compute. We need the energy, the facilities, the chips to support that." His comments arrive at a moment when the AI industry debates whether massive infrastructure spending will outpace actual demand, with some projects already facing write-downs and community opposition.


## CoreWeave Partnership Drives Growth


Gomez's concerns about supply constraints gained credibility from CoreWeave's robust earnings report released the same day. The neocloud provider posted better-than-expected sales of $3.66 billion for the September 2026 quarter, powered partly by its growing relationship with clients including Cohere. This partnership represents a critical lifeline for startups without the capital to build proprietary data center infrastructure.


"We might be over-indexing to fear in this present moment, but hopefully the build-out continues, and those supply pressures do alleviate," Gomez said, acknowledging the industry's nervous tension between expansion costs and genuine operational need.


## Officially Launched on November 11, 2026


Cohere's public position on compute scarcity was officially released on November 11, 2026, during Gomez's visit to Japan. The company is actively expanding relationships with Japanese enterprise customers and government agencies as part of its[sovereign AI](https://emergent.sh/news/ai-definition-battle-reveals-global-power) strategy, which supports nations pursuing domestically controlled artificial intelligence capabilities. Toronto-based Cohere raised as much as $5 billion in an October 2026 funding round that valued the company at more than $20 billion.


## Infrastructure Spending Under Scrutiny


The debate over AI data center buildout intensity has grown sharper as costs escalate and local communities increasingly protest facility construction in their areas. SoftBank Group announced on November 10, 2026 that it was writing down $3.7 billion in costs tied to its Ohio data center project, highlighting the financial risks of infrastructure expansion. Yet Gomez's on-the-ground experience suggests demand still outstrips supply for companies actively deploying AI at scale.


Cohere works closely with Nvidia to develop custom AI models optimized for the chipmaker's platforms. When asked about recent revelations regarding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Gomez called the situation "a really unfortunate episode" and warned that any leadership change involving someone as effective and visionary as Huang would prove "quite disruptive" for an industry heavily dependent on Nvidia's technology roadmap.


## What This Means


Cohere's compute struggle reveals a critical gap between infrastructure capacity fears and operational reality for AI companies. While macro-level spending concerns persist, firms actively training and deploying enterprise models still face severe resource constraints. This tension suggests the market remains far from oversupplied, particularly for companies lacking their own data centers. As sovereign AI initiatives expand globally, compute access will likely remain a competitive bottleneck well into 2027, making partnerships with providers like CoreWeave increasingly strategic for startups competing in the enterprise AI space.
